section.heading: 1.3. New Functions from Old Functions
section.paragraph: In this section we start with the basic functions we discussed in Section 1.2 and obtain new functions by shifting, stretching, and reflecting their graphs. We also show how to combine pairs of functions by the standard arithmetic operations and by composition.
section.heading: Transformations of Functions
section.paragraph: By applying certain transformations to the graph of a given function we can obtain the graphs of related functions. This will give us the ability to sketch the graphs of many functions quickly by hand. It will also enable us to write equations for given graphs.

Let’s first consider translations of graphs. If $$c$$ is a positive number, then the graph of $$y = f(x) + c$$ is just the graph of $$y = f(x)$$ shifted upward a distance of $$c$$ units (because each $$y$$ -coordinate is increased by the same number $$c$$ ). Likewise, if $$g(x) = f(x - c)$$ , where $$c > 0$$ , then the value of $$g$$ at $$x$$ is the same as the value of $$f$$ at $$x - c$$ ( $$c$$ units to the left of $$x$$ ). Therefore the graph of $$y = f(x - c)$$ is just the graph of $$y = f(x)$$ shifted $$c$$ units to the right (see Figure 1).

image.alt: Details The vertical and the horizontal shifts of a function are displayed on the x y coordinate plane. Both the axes are unmarked. The curve labeled y = f(x), begins above the positive x axis in the first quadrant, goes up to the right, concave down, reaches a high point, then goes down and to the right, becoming concave up, reaches its low point, and again goes up and to the right. The same curve is drawn c units rightward and is labeled y = f(x minus c) such that the horizontal distance between y = f(x) and y = f(x minus c) is c units. The same curve y = f(x) is drawn c units leftward and is labeled y = f(x + c) such that the horizontal distance between y = f(x) and y = f(x + c) is c units. The same curve y = f(x) is drawn c units upward and is labeled y = f(x) + c such that the vertical distance between y = f(x) and y = f(x) + c is c units. The same curve y = f(x) is drawn c units downward in the fourth quadrant and is labeled y = f(x) minus c such that the vertical distance between the curves y = f(x) and y = f(x) minus c is c units.

$$\begin{array}{l} {y = f(x) + c, \text{shift the graph of} y = f(x) \text{a distance} c \text{units upward} } \\ {y = f(x) - c, \text{shift the graph of} y = f(x) \text{a distance} c \text{units downward} } \\ {y = f(x - c), \text{shift the graph of} y = f(x) \text{a distance} c \text{units to the right} } \\ {y = f(x + c), \text{shift the graph of} y = f(x) \text{a distance} c \text{units to the left} } \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: Now let’s consider the stretching and reflecting transformations. If $$c > 1$$ , then the graph of $$y = cf(x)$$ is the graph of $$y = f(x)$$ stretched by a factor of $$c$$ in the vertical direction (because each $$y$$ -coordinate is multiplied by the same number $$c$$ ). The graph of $$y = - f(x)$$ is the graph of $$y = f(x)$$ reflected about the $$x$$ -axis because the point $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ is replaced by the point $$\left( {x, - y} \right)$$ . (See Figure 2 and the following chart, where the results of other stretching, shrinking, and reflecting transformations are also given.)

image.alt: Details Four different transformations of a curve are displayed on the x y coordinate plane. Both the axes are unmarked. The curve labeled y = f(x) begins above the positive x axis in the first quadrant, goes up and to the right, concave down, reaches a high point, then goes down and to the right, concave up, reaches a low point, and again goes up and to the right. This curve y = f(x) is reflected about the x axis and the new curve thus formed in the fourth quadrant is labeled y = negative f(x). The curves y = f(x) and y = negative f(x) are equidistant from the x axis such that the low point of y = negative f(x) is located directly below the high point of y = f(x), and the high point of y = negative f(x) is located directly below the low point of y = f(x). The curve y = f(x) is reflected about the y axis and the new curve thus formed in the second quadrant is labeled y = f(negative x). The curves y = f(x) and y = f(negative x) are equidistant from the y axis such that the high point of y = f(negative x) is located directly to the left of the high point of y = f(x), and the low point of y = f(negative x) is located directly to the left of the low point of y = f(x). A curve, which has the same shape as the curve y = f(x), is drawn above it but is taller and a little narrower than f(x). This curve is labeled y = c f(x) where c > 1. Another curve, which has the same shape as the curve y = f(x), is drawn below it, but is shorter and a little wider than y = f(x), and is labeled y = (1/c) f(x). The high points of y = f(x), y = c f(x), and y = (1/c) f(x) lie on the same vertical line. Similarly, the low points of y = f(x), y = c f(x), and y = (1/c) f(x) lie on the same vertical line.

section.paragraph: Figure 3 illustrates these stretching transformations when applied to the cosine function with $$c = 2$$ . For instance, in order to get the graph of $$y = 2\cos x$$ we multiply the $$y$$ -coordinate of each point on the graph of $$y = \cos x$$ by $$2$$ . This means that the graph of $$y = \cos x$$ gets stretched vertically by a factor of $$2$$ .

image.alt: Details Two graphs are displayed, each has three cosine curves on the x y coordinate plane. In both the graphs, the x axis is displayed from 0 to 6 in increments of 1 unit. The curve, y = cos(x), enters the viewing window in the second quadrant, goes up and to the right, reaches its high point at (0, 1), then goes down and to the right through (pi/2, 0), reaches its low point at (pi, negative 1), goes up and to the right by crossing the x axis at (3 pi/2, 0), and reaches its high point at (2 pi, 1), and then goes down and to the right. The curve, y = (1/2) cos(x), enters the second quadrant, reaches its high point at (0, 1/2), falls through (pi/2, 0) to a low point at (pi, negative 1/2), again rises to a high point at (2 pi, 1/2), and the pattern then repeats. This curve is taller and narrower than the first curve.

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Figure 9 shows graphs of the number of hours of daylight as functions of the time of the year at several latitudes. Given that Philadelphia is located at approximately $$40{}_{}^{}$$ latitude, find a function that models the length of daylight at Philadelphia.

image.alt: Details Five curves are graphed on a coordinate plane on the grid lines. The horizontal axis is displayed with months from March to December. The vertical axis labeled Hours is displayed from 0 to 20 in increments of 2 hours. The purple curve which is located at approximately 60 degrees North latitude begins at 12 hours on March 21, reaches its approximate peak at 18.5 hours on June 21, then falls to 12 hours on September 21, and ends with an approximate low point at 5.5 on December 21. The yellow curve which is located at approximately 50 degrees N latitude begins at 12 hours on March 21, reaches its approximate peak at 16.2 hours on June 21, then falls to 12 hours on September 21, and ends with an approximate low point at 7.8 on December 21. The blue curve which is located at approximately 40 degrees North latitude begins at 12 hours on March 21, reaches its approximate peak at 14.8 hours on June 21, then falls to 12 hours on September 21, and ends with an approximate low point at 9.2 hours on December 21. The red curve, which is located at 30 degrees North latitude, begins at 12 hours on March 21, reaches its approximate peak at 14 hours on June 21, then falls to 12 hours on September 21, and ends with an approximate low point at 10 hours on December 21. The black curve, which is located at 20 degrees North latitude, begins at 12 hours on March 21, reaches its approximate peak at 13 hours on June 21, then falls to 12 hours on September 21, and ends with an approximate low point at 11 hours on December 21.

figure.caption: Graph of the length of daylight from March 21 through December 21 at various latitudes

example.paragraph: Solution Notice that each curve resembles a shifted and stretched sine function. By looking at the blue curve we see that, at the latitude of Philadelphia, daylight lasts about $$14.8$$ hours on June 21 and $$9.2$$ hours on December 21, so the amplitude of the curve (the factor by which we have to stretch the sine curve vertically) is $$\frac{1}{2}\left( {14.8 - 9.2} \right) = 2.8$$ .

By what factor do we need to stretch the sine curve horizontally if we measure the time $$t$$ in days? Because there are about $$365$$ days in a year, the period of our model should be $$365$$ . But the period of $$y = \sin t$$ is $$2\pi$$ , so the horizontal stretching factor is $$2\pi \slash 365$$ .

We also notice that the curve begins its cycle on March 21, the $$80$$ th day of the year, so we have to shift the curve $$80$$ units to the right. In addition, we shift it $$12$$ units upward. Therefore we model the length of daylight in Philadelphia on the $$t$$ th day of the year by the function
$$L(t) = 12 + 2.8\sin\left\lbrack {\frac{2\pi}{365}\left( {t - 80} \right)} \right\rbrack$$

section.paragraph: Another transformation of some interest is taking the absolute value of a function. If $$\left. y = \middle| f(x) \right|$$ , then according to the definition of absolute value, $$y = f(x)$$ when $$f(x) \geqslant 0$$ and $$y = - f(x)$$ when $$f(x) < 0$$ . This tells us how to get the graph of $$\left. y = \middle| f(x) \right|$$ from the graph of $$y = f(x)$$ : the part of the graph that lies above the $$x$$ -axis remains the same, and the part that lies below the $$x$$ -axis is reflected about the $$x$$ -axis.

We see that the graph lies below the $$x$$ -axis when $$- 1 < x < 1$$ , so we reflect that part of the graph about the $$x$$ -axis to obtain the graph of $$y = \left| {x^{2} - 1} \right|$$ in Figure 10(b).

section.heading: Combinations of Functions
section.paragraph: Two functions $$f$$ and $$g$$ can be combined to form new functions $$f + g$$ , $$f - g$$ , $$fg$$ , and $$f \slash g$$ in a manner similar to the way we add, subtract, multiply, and divide real numbers.

note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: Given two functions $$f$$ and $$g$$ , the sum, difference, product, and quotient functions are defined by

section.paragraph: If the domain of $$f$$ is $$A$$ and the domain of $$g$$ is $$B$$ , then the domain of $$f + g$$ (and the domain of $$f - g$$ ) is the intersection $$A \cap B$$ because both $$f(x)$$ and $$g(x)$$ have to be defined. For example, the domain of $$f(x) = \sqrt{x}$$ is $$A = \lbrack 0,\infty)$$ and the domain of $$g(x) = \sqrt{2 - x}$$ is $$B = ( - \infty,2\rbrack$$ , so the domain of $$(f + g)(x) = \sqrt{x} + \sqrt{2 - x}$$ is $$A \cap B = \left\lbrack {0,2} \right\rbrack$$ .

The domain of $$fg$$ is also $$A \cap B$$ . Because we can’t divide by $$0$$ , the domain of $$f \slash g$$ is $$\left\{ x \in A \cap B \middle| g(x) \neq 0 \right\}$$ . For instance, if $$f(x) = x^{2}$$ and $$g(x) = x - 1$$ , then the domain of the rational function $$\left( {f \slash g} \right)(x) = x^{2} \slash \left( {x - 1} \right)$$ is $$\left\{ x \middle| x \neq 1 \right\}$$ , or $$\left( {- \infty,1} \right) \cup \left( {1,\infty} \right)$$ .

There is another way of combining two functions to obtain a new function. For example, suppose that $$y = f(u) = \sqrt{u}$$ and $$u = g(x) = x^{2} + 1$$ . Since $$y$$ is a function of $$u$$ and $$u$$ is, in turn, a function of $$x$$ , it follows that $$y$$ is ultimately a function of $$x$$ . We compute this by substitution:
The procedure is called composition because the new function is composed of the two given functions $$f$$ and $$g$$ .

In general, given any two functions $$f$$ and $$g$$ , we start with a number $$x$$ in the domain of $$g$$ and calculate $$g(x)$$ . If this number $$g(x)$$ is in the domain of $$f$$ , then we can calculate the value of $$f\left( {g(x)} \right)$$ . Notice that the output of one function is used as the input to the next function. The result is a new function $$h(x) = f\left( {g(x)} \right)$$ obtained by substituting $$g$$ into $$f$$ . It is called the composition (or composite) of $$f$$ and $$g$$ and is denoted by $$f \circ g$$ (“ $$f$$ circle $$g$$ ”).

section.paragraph: The domain of $$f \circ g$$ is the set of all $$x$$ in the domain of $$g$$ such that $$g(x)$$ is in the domain of $$f$$ . In other words, $$\left( {f \circ g} \right)(x)$$ is defined whenever both $$g(x)$$ and $$f\left( {g(x)} \right)$$ are defined. Figure 11 shows how to picture $$f \circ g$$ in terms of machines.

image.alt: Details A diagram shows two rectangular machines that are arranged vertically and the third rectangular machine on the right side. The machine at the top is labeled g, the machine at the bottom is labeled f, and the machine on the right side is labeled f of g. Each machine has its openings at the top and bottom sides. The top side of the machine g provides an entry x into it with a downward arrow and is labeled Input. Its bottom side provides an exit g(x) with another downward arrow. Now, the function g(x) acts as the input for the machine f, and provides an exit f(g(x)) with a downward arrow and is labeled Output. A curved arrow from machine g provides an input x for the machine f of g at its top side. The arrow then passes through the machine f of g and flows to the output f(g(x)).

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: If $$f(x) = x^{2}$$ and $$g(x) = x - 3$$ , find the composite functions $$f \circ g$$ and $$g \circ f$$ .
Solution We have

$$\begin{array}{lcl} {\left( {f \circ g} \right)(x)} & = & {f\left( {g(x)} \right) = f\left( {x - 3} \right) = \left( {x - 3} \right)^{2}} \\ {\left( {g \circ f} \right)(x)} & = & {g(f(x)) = g(x^{2}) = x^{2} - 3} \end{array}$$

Note You can see from Example 6 that, in general, $$f \circ g \neq g \circ f$$ . Remember, the notation $$f \circ g$$ means that the function $$g$$ is applied first and then $$f$$ is applied second. In Example 6, $$f \circ g$$ is the function that first subtracts $$3$$ and then squares; $$g \circ f$$ is the function that first squares and then subtracts $$3$$ .

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: If $$f(x) = \sqrt{x}$$ and $$g(x) = \sqrt{2 - x}$$ , find each function and its domain.
Solution

list.item: (a) $$\left( {f \circ g} \right)(x) = f\left( {g(x)} \right) = f{(\sqrt{2 - x})} = \sqrt{\sqrt{2 - x}} = \sqrt[4]{2 - x}$$ The domain of $$f \circ g$$ is $$\left\{ x \middle| 2 - x \geqslant 0 \right\} = \left\{ x \middle| x \leqslant 2 \right\} = ( - \infty,2\rbrack$$ .

(b) $$\left( {g \circ f} \right)(x) = g\left( {f(x)} \right) = g\left( \sqrt{x} \right) = \sqrt{2 - \sqrt{x}}$$ For $$\sqrt{x}$$ to be defined we must have $$x \geqslant 0$$ . For $$\sqrt{2 - \sqrt{x}}$$ to be defined we must have $$2 - \sqrt{x} \geqslant 0$$ , that is, $$\sqrt{x} \leqslant 2$$ , or $$x \leqslant 4$$ . Thus we have $$0 \leqslant x \leqslant 4$$ , so the domain of $$g \circ f$$ is the closed interval $$\left\lbrack {0,4} \right\rbrack$$ . If $$0 \leqslant a \leqslant b$$ , then $$a^{2} \leqslant b^{2}$$ .
(c) $$\left( {f \circ f} \right)(x) = f\left( {f(x)} \right) = f\left( \sqrt{x} \right) = \sqrt{\sqrt{x}} = \sqrt[4]{x}$$ The domain of $$f \circ f$$ is $$\lbrack 0,\infty)$$ .

(d) $$\left( {g \circ g} \right)(x) = g\left( {g(x)} \right) = g{(\sqrt{2 - x})} = \sqrt{2 - \sqrt{2 - x}}$$ This expression is defined when both $$2 - x \geqslant 0$$ and $$2 - \sqrt{2 - x} \geqslant 0$$ . The first inequality means $$x \leqslant 2$$ , and the second is equivalent to $$\sqrt{2 - x} \leqslant 2$$ , or $$2 - x \leqslant 4$$ , or $$x \geqslant - 2$$ . Thus $$- 2 \leqslant x \leqslant 2$$ , so the domain of $$g \circ g$$ is the closed interval $$\left\lbrack {- 2,2} \right\rbrack$$ .

example.heading: Example 8
example.paragraph: Find $$f \circ g \circ h$$ if $$f(x) = x \slash \left( {x + 1} \right)$$ , $$g(x) = x^{10}$$ , and $$h(x) = x + 3$$ .
Solution

$$\begin{array}{l} {\left( {f \circ g \circ h} \right)(x) = {f\left( {g\left( {h(x)} \right)} \right) = f\left( {g\left( {x + 3} \right)} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{\left( {f \circ g \circ h} \right)(x)} = {f((x + 3)^{10}) = \frac{(x + 3)^{10}}{(x + 3)^{10} + 1}}} \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: So far we have used composition to build complicated functions from simpler ones. But in calculus it is often useful to be able to decompose a complicated function into simpler ones, as in the following example.

example.heading: Example 9
example.paragraph: Given $$F(x) = \cos^{2}(x + 9)$$ , find functions $$f$$ , $$g$$ , and $$h$$ such that $$F = f \circ g \circ h$$ .
Solution Since $$F(x) = \left\lbrack {\cos\left( {x + 9} \right)} \right\rbrack^{2}$$ , the formula for $$F$$ says: first add $$9$$ , then take the cosine of the result, and finally square. So we let
Then

$$\begin{array}{l} {\left( {f \circ g \circ h} \right)(x) = {f\left( {g\left( {h(x)} \right)} \right) = f\left( {g\left( {x + 9} \right)} \right) = f\left( {\cos\left( {x + 9} \right)} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{\left( {f \circ g \circ h} \right)(x)} = {\left\lbrack \cos(x + 9) \right\rbrack^{2} = F(x)}} \end{array}$$
